subject: physics

moments.title: Rutherford classifies alpha and beta radiation
moments.body:
Rutherford, a New Zealander working at McGill in Montreal, distinguishes two kinds of radiation from uranium: alpha (heavy, slow, stopped by paper) and beta (light, fast, stopped by thin metal). Villard later adds gamma (the most penetrating).

Rutherford goes on to identify alpha particles as helium nuclei.
moments.takeaway: Radioactivity is sorted into types. Rutherford's career as 'the father of nuclear physics' is launched.

moments.title: Geiger and Marsden's startling backscatter
moments.who: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, Manchester
moments.body:
Working under Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fire alpha particles at gold foil. Most pass through with small deflections, consistent with the plum-pudding model. But about 1 in 8000 bounce nearly straight back.

In Rutherford's famous reaction: 'It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.'
moments.takeaway: Backscatter is impossible if the atom's positive charge is spread out smoothly. Something dense and small must be deflecting the alphas.

moments.title: Rutherford's nuclear atom
moments.body:
Rutherford proposes the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons orbiting at relatively huge distance. He calculates the nucleus must have a radius less than 10 to the minus 14 m — far smaller than the atom (10 to the minus 10 m).

Most of the atom is empty space. Atoms are mostly nothing.

quote.text: It was quite the most incredible event that has ever happened to me in my life.
quote.attrib: Ernest Rutherford, on the gold foil results

moments.takeaway: Atoms are mostly empty space. The plum pudding model dies.

moments.title: Chadwick discovers the neutron
moments.body:
Working under Rutherford, Chadwick is puzzled by a 'radiation' from beryllium bombarded by alpha particles. The radiation has no charge but knocks protons out of paraffin. Calculation: it must be a neutral particle of about the proton's mass.

Chadwick gets the Nobel Prize in 1935. The neutron explains why isotopes exist and underwrites the entire chemistry of nuclei.
moments.takeaway: The nucleus contains protons AND neutrons. The structure of matter is now mostly mapped out.

moments.title: Deep inelastic scattering — protons have parts
moments.body:
High-energy electrons fired at protons at SLAC scatter at sharper angles than a smooth proton would allow — exactly the same kind of evidence as Rutherford's gold foil, just at higher energy. The protons contain tiny pointlike scatterers.

These are quarks, predicted by Gell-Mann and Zweig in 1964. The Nobel-Prize-winning analysis (Friedman, Kendall, Taylor, 1990) confirms quark structure.
moments.takeaway: The pattern repeats. Rutherford's atomic substructure is mirrored at the next scale down.

now.title: Nuclear physics today
now.body:
We know about 3,000 isotopes of 118 elements. Nuclear reactors, medical isotopes, ion beam therapy and nuclear weapons all build on Rutherford's nuclear atom. Quark/gluon structure of nucleons is described by quantum chromodynamics — confirmed at the LHC and elsewhere.

The nuclear chart still has frontier regions: superheavy nuclei (elements 119 and beyond) and exotic neutron-rich nuclei produced at facilities like FRIB (Michigan).
now.open_questions: Where does the 'island of stability' for superheavy elements lie? What's the neutron-rich limit of stable nuclei? What happens inside neutron stars (giant atomic nuclei)? Can we image the internal structure of protons more directly?

reflection: Rutherford was a brilliant experimentalist and an opinionated administrator. He won the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (despite being a physicist) and famously remarked: 'In science there is only physics; all the rest is stamp collecting.' How do disciplinary rivalries shape who claims which discoveries?
